advisor.summary: A cost segregation study re-documents a building's depreciable basis: an engineering analysis carves §1245 personalty (5/7-year) and 15-year land improvements out of the §1250 shell, letting the short-life components ride 100% bonus depreciation under §168(k) in the placed-in-service year. Hospital Corp. of America legitimized component-based lives inside a building; the IRS's own Cost Segregation Audit Techniques Guide sets the quality bar a study must clear. For property already in service, the missed depreciation lands all at once as a §481(a) adjustment on Form 3115 — no amended returns. The exercise is a timing-and-character trade: value turns on the client's ability to use the loss currently (REPS, short-term-rental treatment, other passive income), and the accelerated basis comes back as recapture on a taxable exit. The engine models the study as a first-year acceleration against rental income, with §469 gating applied downstream.
mechanics: The study allocates acquisition or construction cost across 5/7-year §1245 personal property (flooring, cabinetry, specialty electrical and plumbing, equipment hookups), 15-year land improvements (paving, site utilities, landscaping), and the remaining §1250 building shell on its 27.5- or 39-year straight line.

Everything shifted to a 20-year-or-shorter life is qualified property for 100% bonus under §168(k), so the reclassified slice — commonly 15–35% of depreciable basis, depending on property type — deducts in the placed-in-service year.

For buildings already in service, Rev. Proc. 2015-13's automatic method-change procedures deliver the full catch-up as a one-year §481(a) adjustment on Form 3115 filed with a timely return — prior years stay closed.

Whether the resulting loss is usable is a separate §469 question: real estate professional status, short-term-rental treatment, other passive income, or the $25,000 active-participation allowance supply the paths; without one, the loss suspends and carries forward.

The model applies the study’s first-year acceleration against the rental activity and nothing more — recapture, the later-year depreciation give-back, and the study fee live in the plan narrative, not the engine.

authority.note: The Service’s quality bar: engineering-based studies with documented takeoffs outrank residual and rule-of-thumb allocations.

requirements: Depreciable building basis owned by the taxpayer — land never qualifies, and the land/building split should be defensible before the study prices components.
An engineering-based study that meets the Audit Techniques Guide standard, with the workpapers retained.
A current-year path to using the loss (REPS, short-term-rental treatment, passive income, or the active-participation allowance) — confirmed before the fee is spent.
For in-service property, a Form 3115 filed with a timely return for the year of change.
risks: The leading audit theory is allocation quality: percentage guesses and aggressive personalty splits get re-worked at exam under the Audit Techniques Guide — Hospital Corp. of America protects the method, not any particular number.
Losses trapped by §469 turn an expensive study into a deferred benefit — screen the loss path before commissioning the study.
Acceleration comes back at exit: §1245 recapture at ordinary rates on the personalty and unrecaptured §1250 gain at 25% on the rest — the exit plan (hold, 1031, step-up at death) belongs in the file.
Study fees running several thousand dollars must clear the modeled benefit at the client’s actual marginal rate.
State decoupling from bonus depreciation can strand the state benefit on a far slower schedule than the federal one.
stateNotes: Conformity: confirm every state in the footprint conforms to §168(k) before quoting a combined benefit — decoupled states add back the bonus and recover it over their own schedules.
Missouri conforms to federal depreciation through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121), so the accelerated deduction flows into the Missouri return without addback.

PTET interaction: where the property sits in a pass-through with a PTET election, the accelerated deduction shrinks the PTET base — sequence the projection so the state tax and the federal deduction are not double-counted.
reviewChecklist: Passive-loss path confirmed and documented before the study was commissioned.
Study is engineering-based, from a reputable firm, with allocation percentages inside observed ranges for the property type.
Land/building allocation reconciled with the study so land value is never depreciated.
In-service properties: Form 3115 prepared, §481(a) adjustment computed, and the filing calendared with the timely return.
Modeled first-year acceleration ties to the study report, with recapture exposure noted in the client’s permanent file.

client.teaser: An engineering study can pull years of property deductions into this one.
client.headline: Find the fast write-offs hiding inside your building
plainEnglish: A building gets deducted slowly — over 27 to 39 years. But much of what you paid for is not really 'building.' Carpet, cabinets, wiring for equipment, parking lots, and landscaping all count as faster assets under the tax rules.

A cost segregation study is an engineering report that finds those pieces and puts a price on each. Once they are identified, most can be deducted right away under current law. The result is often one very large deduction now instead of small ones for decades.

It even works on buildings you already own. A special catch-up filing collects the missed deductions in one year, with no amended returns. First, though, we check that you can actually use the deduction now — that depends on your other income and how you run the property.
client.analogy: It is like unpacking a moving box labeled 'house' and finding tools, rugs, and appliances inside — each one can be claimed on its own faster schedule.
benefits: A large first-year deduction, often 15% to 35% of the building's cost
Works on buildings you already own, through a one-time catch-up filing
Frees up cash now to reinvest or pay down debt
The study report doubles as your audit support
steps: WE confirm your tax picture lets you use the deduction this year — before you spend a dollar.
WE engage the engineering firm and vet its allocation report.
WE file the return, plus the catch-up form if the building is already in service.
YOU provide closing statements, construction invoices, and property access for the study.
clientCommitments: Share purchase and construction records with the engineers
Keep the study report with your permanent tax records
Talk with us before selling the property — these deductions change the tax on a sale

annualMaintenance: Update depreciation schedules for the study's component lives each year
Re-test the passive-loss path each year before layering on further accelerations
Track recapture exposure in the permanent file as basis burns down
deliverables: Cost segregation feasibility memo weighing the modeled benefit against the study fee
Engineering study report and reconciled depreciation schedules
Form 3115 with §481(a) computation for in-service property
